problems.stem: A candidate planned a flipped lesson where students watch a video at home and use class time for an AI-coached problem set. After teaching it once, only 9 of 26 students had watched the video. Which revision is driven by the field evidence rather than by the candidate's preference?
options: Keep the flipped plan because the design is sound in principle.
Move the video to a 7-minute in-class viewing because most students lacked reliable at-home time and the AI coaching assumed they had watched it.
Assign the same video again and warn students to watch it.
Add a quiz penalty for students who did not watch.
problems.explanation: The field evidence (17 of 26 did not watch at home) points to an access barrier, so the defensible revision moves the video into class. Repeating the plan or adding penalties ignores the evidence.

problems.stem: After one rough lesson, the candidate wants to scrap the whole AI-coached problem set. What does responsible revision require before that large a change?
options: Scrap it immediately because one lesson felt chaotic.
Separate which part actually failed (the at-home prep) from the part that worked (in-class coaching) so she revises the cause, not the whole plan.
Replace it with a tool the candidate personally prefers.
Blame the students for not preparing and keep everything the same.
problems.explanation: Revision after field evidence isolates the failing component instead of discarding everything. The candidate should change the cause (prep access), not abandon a part that worked.

problems.stem: The candidate gives an AI tool her lesson plan and the line that only 9 students watched the video, and asks for a revision. The AI proposes a gamified points system but never addresses home access. How should she use it?
options: Adopt the gamified system because the AI is good at engagement ideas.
Note that the AI ignored the access cause she observed, and revise toward the access barrier instead of the AI's engagement framing.
Trust that gamification will fix attendance to the video.
Ask the AI to add more game mechanics.
problems.explanation: The AI reframed an access problem as an engagement problem. The candidate's field evidence about home access must govern the revision, not the AI's default framing.

problems.stem: What record best shows the candidate's revision was evidence-based rather than a hunch?
options: A note that the second lesson felt better.
The original plan, the field data that prompted the change, the specific revision, and the follow-up data showing whether participation rose.
A statement that the candidate has more experience now.
problems.explanation: Evidence-based revision shows the original plan, the prompting data, the change, and follow-up data. A feeling that it went better is not evidence the revision worked.
